Software

Files and folders


WizTree
Scans entire directories, folders and subfolders, and shows a treemap of where files are taking up space, among other things. I used to recommend TreeSize Free, but WizTree is faster and doesn’t push the paid version as much.


Path Length Checker deadlydog on GitHub
A stand-alone app that lists the path and length of every file and directory in a folder. Handy for tracking down Windows paths that are too long for some programs to handle.


Beyond Compare
File and folder comparison: versions by date or folder, folder structure, and line-level differences in text files. It also syncs one folder to another.


7-Zip
Unzips files, with more options than the standard Windows unzip. Handy.

See also: Collaborative Lesson Development Training, The Carpentries Incubator, The Carpentries Lab


Collaborative Lesson Development Training
The Carpentries’ own course on building a lesson as an open source project: lesson design, collaborating on one, and the lesson infrastructure. Teams of two to five work on a single real lesson across six half-days, and at least one person per team needs Instructor Training or Learner-Centered Teaching first.
See also: The Carpentries Incubator, The Carpentries Lab


The Carpentries Incubator
Where community members develop lessons in the open, before any review. Plenty is taught from here already; treat it as work in progress rather than as vetted material.


The Carpentries Lab
The peer-reviewed tier: short-format lessons that have been through review and follow the Carpentries lesson design. Review here can also produce a paper in the Journal of Open Source Education, which mints a DOI, so a lesson becomes a citable peer-reviewed publication rather than only a teaching resource. Submission is by invitation while the review process is piloted.

title: Research interests
text:
Skip to main content





Measurement & psychometrics. How well we measure things drives everything downstream. I work on scale scoring and missing-data decisions (person-mean imputation, prorated scale scores, completeness thresholds), measurement invariance, and structural equation and item response models.
Privacy-preserving synthetic data. With NSWERS, I generate synthetic versions of large, longitudinal administrative datasets and evaluate how faithfully they reproduce the original data (tidysynthesis, syntheval). The goal is analysis that does not expose individuals: as much a question of what can safely be released as of how well the synthesis works.
Applied evaluation & public policy research. At the NEAR Center and the Public Policy Center, I support program evaluation and policy research for state agencies and community partners, from study design and survey methods through analysis and reporting.
Research data infrastructure. Documentation, variable lineage, and reproducible pipelines: the tooling that lets teams trust and reuse their data. This is where my software comes from.
Youth physical activity & exercise physiology. Earlier work covered neuromuscular fatigue, high-intensity interval training, and physical performance testing. See publications.

Amelia Miramonti, PhD, is a postdoctoral researcher at the Nebraska Evaluation and Research (NEAR) Center and adjunct faculty in the Department of Educational Psychology at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln. She also supports applied research for Nebraska state agencies and communities with the University of Nebraska Public Policy Center, and develops privacy-preserving synthetic datasets from administrative records with the Nebraska Statewide Workforce and Educational Reporting System (NSWERS). She holds an interdisciplinary PhD from the University of Nebraska–Lincoln (2025) that combined quantitative, qualitative, and psychometric methods with exercise physiology and nutrition, an MA in Quantitative, Qualitative, and Psychometric Methods from the same institution, and a BSc and MSc in sport and exercise science from the University of Central Florida. Her more than 30 peer-reviewed articles range from neuromuscular physiology, strength and conditioning, and sports nutrition to child nutrition and career psychology. LSPC Weather
React, TypeScript, and Vite
A skydiving weather dashboard for the Lincoln Sport Parachute Club at Brown’s Airport (NE69) in Weeping Water, Nebraska, tuned to the club’s Cessna 182 jump plane. It folds a three-site manual routine (NOAA hourly forecast, cloud forecast, and the KPMV METAR) into one page, and adds winds aloft for freefall drift and density altitude for jump-plane climb.
It flags seven conditions: surface wind, the club waiver’s gust ceiling, visibility, FAA flight category, overcast sky, a thunderstorm reported in the METAR, and parachute ops between sunset and sunrise. Each one fires only on a published limit, from the USPA SIM, the CFRs, the FAA’s AIM, or the club’s posted waiver, or on a plain observed fact, and cites the source it rests on. Where nothing published sets a threshold, nothing fires: no invented numbers, and no go/no-go verdict. Everything else, winds aloft and density altitude included, is a reading to judge for yourself.
In development, and not endorsed by USPA, LSPC, or any licensed professional. Jump decisions stay with the jumper, the Safety and Training Advisor, and the pilot in command.

pleasantry
R package
Started at posit::conf(2026) in Houston, in Hadley Wickham and Jenny Bryan’s Modern R workflow (ft. Positron and AI) workshop on Monday, September 14, and carried on from there. compliment() assembles a line from template, adjective, and subject banks, steered by a weirdness scale running sincere to quirky to bizarre, a mood (sincere, grumpy, cheerful, or dramatic), a profanity level that includes a deliberately silly clean tier, and a shakespearean flag for pseudo-Elizabethan phrasing. farewell() handles the goodbyes, drawing a whole phrase from its own mood bank rather than composing one, and takes the same options apart from weirdness. compliment_of_the_day() and farewell_of_the_day() each return one result that is fixed for a given date and leave the global random seed alone.
Both the workshop original and the later work on it were AI-assisted, which is worth being specific about rather than leaving to the workshop’s title. The original package was written in the workshop with Positron’s Posit Assistant, on credit allocated for the conference. The rename from compliment, the move to the repository root, and a round of defect fixes afterwards were done with Claude: among them seven templates that hardcoded a before a randomly drawn word, so the Shakespearean mode would emit O, what a eldritch familiar thou dost possess!
Most of the effort went into making the composed compliments read like English: rejecting an adjective the chosen template already uses, resampling adjective and subject pairs that share a word stem (“creative” with “creativity”), and singularizing the subject banks so the Shakespearean blends stopped emitting “Thy vapours is.” The weirdness scale draws each component independently with triangular weights, so a value between tiers blends them instead of flipping over. Note that the strong profanity tier ships explicit language in the package source.

title: JumpStart research summary
text:
Skip to main content








HerPath · 2026 JumpStart Challenge
Helping more women-founded companies in Lincoln get funded and grow: the research
The evidence behind our pitch, what our Lincoln pilot survey heard, and the wider research we read.



Highlights
Research cited in the pitch
Survey results
The rest of the research
Sources




Highlights
Seven findings from across this page.
Each links to a card further down; open the card for the detail, the source and how strong the evidence is.


11% vs 23%
Only 11% of women-owned Nebraska businesses have employees, against 23% of men-owned.1
Lincoln shows the same gap: 13% against 23%.2


27% vs 23%
When women's deals reach US angel investors, 27% get funded, against 23% of all deals.3
The comparison is with the whole market, not with men's deals alone.


78%
Most women-owned employer firms did not ask for credit: 78% did not apply for new credit in 2024.4
Once they apply, women's full-approval rate is close to men's (49% against 52% in 2025).5


Who invests
More women writing checks moved money to women founders.6
When US venture firms hired more women investors, the share of funded founders who were women rose; male investors did not become more likely to back women.


18 of 33
In our pilot survey, the connection people wish for most is a mentor who has done it before.7


14 of 26
The top reason a wanted connection did not happen: “I didn't know who the right person was.”7


10 of 21 women
Caregiving takes up time for 10 of 21 women who answered, and for fewer than 3 of 19 men.7


The survey figures come from a small pilot that reached the team's own contacts; read them as illustrations, not estimates for Lincoln. See what the survey can and cannot tell us.


Back to top

Research cited in the pitch
These are the six facts our pitch rests on, in the order we say them.
Open a card to see where each figure comes from, where to find it in the source, and how we checked it.
Where our pitch wording says more than the source does, the card says so.


Women own 44% of Nebraska businesses1
In the pitch: the spoken script opens with "Women own 44% of Nebraska businesses."
What the source says: the U.S. Small Business Administration's 2025 profile of Nebraska says women made up 47% of workers and owned 44% of businesses.1
The figures come from Census surveys of 2022.
Where to find it: page 3 of the profile, in the part on business ownership share by demographic group.
How we checked: Checked We read the figure in our saved copy of the profile PDF.
Read with care: the profile notes that "Ownership shares include equal and majority ownership."
So the 44% counts businesses owned equally by a woman and a man as well as those mostly owned by women.
Counting only businesses owned mostly by women, the share is about 37% (our arithmetic from the profile's table: 67,994 of the 185,360 businesses with an owner's sex recorded).1



Only 11% of women-owned Nebraska businesses have employees; for men it is 23%, about double1
In the pitch: slide 2 says "Only 11% of women-owned businesses in Nebraska grow to the point of hiring anyone. For men, it's double that."
The script adds the men's figure: twenty-three percent, and says the pilot survey is too small to test that gap.
What the source says: of 67,994 Nebraska businesses owned by women, 7,494 (11%) have employees.
Of 103,863 owned by men, 23,363 (23%) do.1
Of 13,503 owned equally by women and men, 7,103 (53%) have employees.1
23% is a little more than twice 11%.
The figures are for 2022.
Where to find it: page 3 of the profile, in the table of business counts by owner demographic group or location type, rows Female and Male, and the row below them for businesses owned equally by both groups.
How we checked: Checked We read both rows in our saved copy of the profile PDF.
We read the equally owned row there too.
Newer Census figures for 2023 tell the same story: 11% of women-owned Nebraska businesses had employees, against 22% of men-owned (our arithmetic from the Census counts).8
Read with care: the source counts businesses that have employees at one point in time.
It does not follow businesses over time, so it does not show how many tried to grow and could not.
Some owners choose to stay small; why the gap exists is covered under the rest of the research.



When women get in front of angel investors, 27% of their deals get funded, against 23% across the whole market3
In the pitch: slide 3 says "When women get in front of angel investors nationally, they get funded more often than average!"
The slide gives the same two figures.
What the source says: the University of New Hampshire's Center for Venture Research estimates the US angel market each year.
For 2024 it reports that "the yield rate for women entrepreneurs seeking angel capital was 26.7%", above the 23% rate for the market as a whole.3
The yield rate is the share of deals brought to angel investors that end in an investment.
Where to find it: page 1 of the two-page report, in the part on yield rates (23%) and the part on women and minority entrepreneurs and investors (27%).
How we checked: Checked We read both figures in our saved copy of the report.
Read with care: the comparison is with all deals, which include women's, not with men's deals alone.
The figures are national, not for Nebraska.
The two-page report does not give the number of deals behind each rate.
The report reads the higher rate as a sign that women's deals were of high quality.
Our pitch draws a related point: the hard part is getting in the room, not the ideas.
That second step is our reading, not the report's.



In a large trial on an online mentoring platform, only 14% of new users had a real back-and-forth with a mentor9
In the pitch: the script says "In one large experiment on an online mentoring platform, only 14% of new users had a meaningful exchange with a mentor within a few months."
What the source says: Lall, Chen and Mason ran a randomised trial with 3,022 entrepreneurs who joined an online mentoring platform (MicroMentor) between May and August 2019.
39% started at least one conversation with a mentor, but "only 14% have developed a meaningful connection".9
A meaningful connection means four or more messages in one conversation between the entrepreneur and a mentor.
Women were less likely than men to start a conversation with a mentor (a statistically significant difference in the study's main model); the study found no such difference in making a meaningful connection.
One of the trial's three approaches showed new users a video of a successful mentoring relationship.
For women, the study reports: "The chance of a female entrepreneur reaching out to a mentor is increased by 57% after she watches the video."
But the video did not raise their chance of a meaningful connection.9
The 57% is a relative increase, not 57 percentage points, and it counts all women offered the video, whether or not they watched it.
Where to find it: section 4 (Analysis), first paragraph (the 14% and 39%); section 3.2 (Variables), on what counts as a connection; Tables 3 and 4 in section 4 and the text beside them, on the difference between women and men and on the video.
How we checked: Checked We read the figures and the definition in our saved copy of the full article, which is open access.
Read with care: the study describes one platform's new users, not founders in general.
The people in the study were new users of one platform, writing in English or Spanish, and 31% were women, so they are not "founders" in general.
They were followed for about three to six months, not "ever".
And 39% did start a conversation; the 14% is for an exchange of at least four messages.



Our survey: the top reason a connection did not happen was "I didn't know who the right person was", for 14 of 26 who answered7
In the pitch: the script says "We surveyed 48 people in our startup network. The top reason a connection didn't happen: 'I didn't know who the right person was.'"
What the source says: Our pilot survey had 48 responses: 23 from women, 24 from men and 1 with no gender given.
26 of them answered the question on why they could not make the connections they wanted, choosing as many reasons as applied.
14 of the 26 chose "I didn't know who the right person was", more than any other reason (women 7 of 14, men 7 of 12).7
It was the most common reason among both the women and the men who answered.
Where to find it: survey question "What was the reason you weren't able to make these connections?"
How we checked: Checked Counted from the survey responses by script, and the figure was checked a second time with a separate script.
Read with care: the survey reached the team's own contacts, so these counts describe the people who answered, not all Lincoln founders.
The groups are small, so no difference between women and men here can be called a gender difference.
The 48 responses include one test response from our team; without it, this is still the most common reason.



Our survey: the connection people wish for most is "a mentor who's done it before", for 18 of 33 who answered7
In the pitch: slide 3 asks "What do they want most? A mentor who's done it before." The script says the same.
What the source says: 33 people answered the question on which connections they wish they had, choosing as many as applied.
18 of the 33 chose "A mentor who's done it before", more than any other connection (women 10 of 16, men 8 of 17).7
It was the most common choice among both the women and the men who answered.
Where to find it: survey question "Which connections do you wish you had?"
How we checked: Checked Counted from the survey responses by script, and the figure was checked a second time with a separate script.

The rest of the research
Beyond the figures in our pitch, we logged about 300 sources on women business owners, capital, mentoring and programs.
Here are the key findings, grouped by topic.
Each card shows the headline first; open it for the detail, how strong the evidence is, and the source.
Most of this evidence is national or from other countries; where it is about Nebraska or Lincoln, the card says so.
Sources already covered in "Research cited in the pitch" are pointed to rather than repeated.


Capital: loans, grants and investment


Nebraska lenders cover loans from $1,000 to $5 million, but nothing lays them out as one path12
A Lincoln owner can find 0% Kiva loans ($1,000 to $15,000), SBA microloans through Community Development Resources ($1,000 to $50,000), the Nebraska Enterprise Fund ($1,000 to $150,000), Center for Rural Affairs loans ($1,000 to $250,000) and SBA 504 loans through NEDCO for buildings and equipment (up to $5 million).12
None of the pages we read sets these out as a route by business stage or size, so an owner has to work out for herself which one fits.
How strong: loan terms are what each lender states on its own website, read in November 2026.



Only one women-specific source of capital found in Nebraska: a crowdfunding portal for raises of $150,000 to $5 million13
AeQuitas Invest (AQi), based in Omaha, hosts only companies that are at least 50% women-owned, raising $150,000 to $5 million a year through regulated crowdfunding.13
Almost every other Nebraska source of capital we found is open to everyone, not aimed at women.
Repeated searches found no women's angel group, women-led fund, women's grant or women's pitch competition in Nebraska.
How strong: "not found" after several searches in November 2026, not proof that none exists.



78% of women-owned employer firms did not apply for new credit in 20244
In the Census Bureau's national survey, 13% of women-owned businesses with employees applied for new credit in 2024, 78% did not, and 9% did not know.
Of those that applied, 53% got all they asked for, 28% some and 8% none.
Community development lenders (CDFIs) supplied credit to only about 1% of those that got it.4
This points to not applying, rather than being turned down, as a large part of the story.
The source gives no figure for men-owned firms to compare.
How strong: national federal survey, preliminary estimates; no Nebraska figure was checked.



When a development bank shared lenders' risk, women's share of business lending rose by about 23%14
In Türkiye, a development bank lent to five commercial banks on condition they lent on to women-led small businesses, covered first losses up to 10% of each bank's portfolio, and trained bank staff.
In two years, participating banks raised women's share of their business lending by 2 percentage points on average, a rise of almost a quarter from a base of about 9%.
Half of the rise came from new borrowers, and first-time women borrowers were as likely to repay as others.14
How strong: a careful before-and-after comparison using the national credit registry, read in the bank's four-page brief; the brief does not separate the effect of the risk cover from the credit lines and training.



Changing loan terms changed results for women: a two-month repayment grace period raised long-run profits, and also defaults15
In a trial in India, giving women borrowers two months before their first repayment led to more business investment and higher long-run profits, but more of them defaulted.15
In a small trial in Ethiopia, judging loan applications on a psychometric test instead of fixed collateral improved women's access to credit and their businesses' survival, with little sign of growth.16
How strong: both are randomised trials outside the US.
The India result was read at abstract level.
For Ethiopia we give only the direction of the effect, because the draft that holds the figures asks not to be cited.




Networks and mentoring


A local mentor raised women's business profits by about 20%, but only while the pair kept meeting17
In Kenya, women running small businesses who were paired with an experienced local businesswoman raised their profits by about 20%, while a business class did not help.
The gains faded as pairs stopped meeting, and lasted for pairs still meeting after a year.17
In an earlier version of the study, 45% of pairs were still meeting after twelve months, and mentees said nearly 70% of the matches that ended were ended by the mentor.17
How strong: randomised trial with 372 women, outside the US.



Women mentored by women in Uganda raised sales 32% and profits 31%; a second trial points the other way18
In one trial, women entrepreneurs mentored remotely by a woman raised sales 32% and profits 31%, while women mentored by a man did not improve significantly; mentor gender made no difference for men.18
The women-with-women group was small: 48 in the final analysis.
A second Uganda trial, of group mentoring on top of a cash grant, found mentoring did not help women overall.
Its draft brief reports lower profits for women in all-women groups with a woman mentor, while its full paper finds no significant difference between men and women mentors for women.19
The two trials differ in design (one-to-one and remote against group mentoring with cash), so they are best read as disagreeing, not as one cancelling the other.
How strong: two randomised trials, both outside the US, with different results.



Signing up is not being mentored: only 27% of surveyed users of an online mentoring platform had received mentoring20
In a 2020 evaluation of MicroMentor, 27% of 894 surveyed entrepreneurs had been mentored.
Among those who had not, 28% said a mentor never replied and 23% did not know how to contact one.20
In a UK survey, 39% of small firms that had never used a mentor did not know where they would find one.21
The randomised trial on the same platform that our pitch cites found the same bottleneck; see Research cited in the pitch.
How strong: an evaluation commissioned by the platform's funder, mostly of users in developing countries, and a UK government survey of 902 firms; observational.
The report is not consistent on whether the 28% and 23% are shares of users who had not been mentored or of all surveyed users.



Group formats can match one-to-one help at lower cost: group consulting cost about a third as much per firm22
In Colombia, consulting delivered to groups of firms raised sales, profits and productivity at about a third of the cost of one-to-one consulting (US$10,500 against US$28,950 per firm), whose effects were weaker.22
In China, monthly meetings among small groups of business owners, with no mentor, raised revenue 8%, and the gain lasted a year after the meetings ended.23
In Kenya, mentoring added to a cash grant only marginally improved results, and cash alone cost less per dollar of extra profit (US$3.43 against US$4.56).19
How strong: randomised trials outside the US; the Kenya cash result is from a draft research brief.



Mentors' time is the scarce resource: SCORE, a national volunteer mentoring network, asks for 10 to 12 hours a month and caps new requests each week24
SCORE asks mentors for 10 to 12 hours a month, lets them pause for up to 30 days, and since November 2025 limits how many new requests each mentor receives a week, hiding mentors who have reached their limit.24
How programs back their volunteers matters too: on one online platform, corporate-recruited mentors given intensive support did well, while those given only light support did worse than those given none at all (2,344 mentors).25
How strong: SCORE's rules are its own published procedures, with no data on whether they keep mentors longer; the platform study is observational.



Lincoln has several pools of mentors, but few published counts: SCORE reports 61 volunteers across Nebraska26
SCORE has two Nebraska chapters, Lincoln and Greater Omaha, with 61 volunteers statewide in its 2024 figures; no Lincoln-only count was found.26
The University of Nebraska-Lincoln reports mentors supporting student entrepreneurs rising from 165 to 252 in one year, all for UNL students.27
NMotion, Lincoln's accelerator, takes six companies per cohort.28
How strong: each organisation's own figures, not independently checked.




Program models elsewhere


A free growth program for established owners: 57% of graduates reported adding jobs within 30 months29
Goldman Sachs 10,000 Small Businesses teaches owners of existing businesses to plan for growth.
In its 2018 impact report, 45% of participants were women, and 57% of alumni reported adding jobs at 30 months, against 25% of small businesses in a national survey used as a benchmark.29
It is free to participants, and it now accepts applicants from Omaha through a regional cohort.
How strong: self-reported follow-up surveys; no randomised or matched comparison group, and no results by gender.



In the UK, investors who report founder gender backed teams with a woman founder in 33% of deals, against 25% in the wider market30
The UK's Investing in Women Code asks investors and lenders to report each year who they fund.
By March 2026 it had 337 signatories.
In 2025, 33% of signatories' venture deals went to teams with at least one woman founder, against 25% in the wider market, and community lenders that signed made 37% of their business loans to women-led firms.30
How strong: government-published annual figures; firms choose to sign, so the gap does not prove the Code caused it.



A Wisconsin women's lender: 69% of its borrowers were still in business after five years, against 50% nationally31
The Wisconsin Women's Business Initiative Corporation, founded in 1987, combines small loans with training and coaching.
A third-party study released in 2022 found 69% of its borrowers still in business after five years, against 50% nationally, and 70% of borrowers who came with poor credit improved their score.31
How strong: compared with population averages, not with similar businesses, and not split by gender.



Canada's grants to women-owned firms: 41% of recipients reported hiring, but support groups stopped when the money ended32
Canada's Women Entrepreneurship Strategy gave grants of up to C$100,000 to 322 women-owned firms and funded 52 support organisations.
41% of grant recipients reported hiring more staff.
The evaluators found that no new businesses were funded, because two years of accounts were required, and that many support organisations stopped their services when the funding ended.32
How strong: government evaluation based on recipients' own reports, with no comparison group.



Ireland's development agency went from 1 in 10 to more than 1 in 3 supported start-ups led by women33
Enterprise Ireland paired a start-up fund for women-led companies with a women's accelerator from 2012.
By 2017, more than one in three start-ups it supported were led by women, against one in ten in 2012, and 46% of that year's start-fund investments went to women-led companies.33
The women-only fund's last call closed in 2021; a women founders' accelerator continues.
How strong: the agency's own figures, which it credits to its targeted programs; not an independent evaluation.



A Hawai'i accelerator pays each founder a $4,000 care stipend; no Nebraska program found pays for childcare34
Hawai'i FoundHer gives each founder a $20,000 grant and a $4,000 stipend for child or elder care during its six-month program.34
We found no program in Nebraska, or any national online program, that pays for or provides childcare for founders; Nebraska programs fit around caregiving, if at all, through online or part-time formats.
How strong: program terms from its website; the absence in Nebraska is "not found" in our searches.




Evidence on the funding gap


Once women-owned firms apply for a loan, the approval gap is small and changes direction: 49% against 52% got the full amount in 20255
In the Federal Reserve's national survey of businesses with employees, the share of women-owned firms that got the full amount they applied for was 49% in 2025 (men-owned 52%), 54% in 2024 (men-owned 50%) and 45% in 2022 (men-owned 55%).5
The larger gaps sit earlier: in having employees at all (see Research cited in the pitch) and in applying at all (see the capital cards above).
How strong: large national survey, read from the Federal Reserve's own data series; there is no Nebraska breakdown.



More women writing checks moved money to women founders; persuading men did not6
After a high-profile 2015 lawsuit, US venture firms hired more women investors, and the share of funded founders who were women rose.
The rise was "driven entirely by the hiring of female venture capitalists"; male investors did not become more likely to back women.6
On an online investing platform where every investor saw the same profiles, women-led startups did less well with male investors and better with female investors.35
Women were 39% of active US angel investors in 2024, according to the angel market report also used in Research cited in the pitch.3
How strong: two US studies, a journal article read through its authors' summary and a working paper read at abstract level; both observational. The 39% is the angel report's own count.



Investors ask men about gains and women about risks; startups asked mostly about gains raised $16.8 million on average, against $2.3 million36
At a major US startup competition (189 startups, 2010 to 2016), investors tended to ask men questions about gains and growth and women questions about risks and losses.
Startups asked mostly about gains raised $16.8 million on average, against $2.3 million, and each extra question about risks meant $3.8 million less, which fully accounted for gender's effect on funding.
In a follow-up experiment, founders who answered risk questions by talking about gains raised more.36
How strong: peer-reviewed field study plus experiment, US, high-growth tech startups; checked against the published paper.



With identical pitches, 68% chose to fund the one narrated by a man37
In an experiment, 356 of 521 participants (68%) chose to fund the pitch voiced by a man when the words were the same.
In real pitch competitions, male entrepreneurs were 60% more likely to win.37
How strong: peer-reviewed US study from 2014, so dated; checked against the published paper.



At first contact, investors replied with interest 9% more often to women38
In an experiment, 80,000 pitch emails from fictitious founders went to about 28,000 venture investors and angels.
Only 4% got an interested reply, and emails from women got a 9% higher rate of interested replies than identical emails from men.38
So the barrier does not seem to be the first written contact; the evidence points more to who is in the room and how women are received there.
How strong: randomised field experiment, US and international investors, 2018; read in the 2019 working paper.



Loan officers asked for a guarantor 26% more often when the same application came from a woman39
In an experiment with 334 loan officers at a large Turkish bank, approval rates did not differ, but officers were 26% more likely to require a guarantor when an identical application came from a woman; the gap sat mostly with young, inexperienced officers.39
At an Albanian microlender, first-time borrowers assigned a loan officer of the other sex paid 38 basis points more a year and were 10% less likely to apply for a second loan.40
How strong: one randomised and one quasi-random study, both outside the US; the Turkish result read at abstract level.




Gaps in what exists


The rural women's business center that covers Lincoln went from four staff to one41
Lincoln's startup hub is framed around startups and names no women's resource, and Nebraska's two women's business centers are based in Omaha and Grand Island.
The Center for Rural Affairs center, whose service area includes Lincoln, had four staff in 2020 and one full-time person in 2026, and two more Nebraska centers announced in January 2025, one for child care businesses, were never funded.41
So there is no Lincoln front door for women who own businesses but do not call themselves founders.
How strong: the center's own account; the Lincoln picture comes from our review of local program pages.



Women's business centers help people start, not grow: clients' growth and access to capital were lower than similar non-clients'42
The SBA's 2025 evaluation of its women's business centers compared clients with similar businesses that did not use them.
Clients started more businesses, but "business growth outcomes and access to capital declined on average", and businesses they started employed fewer people.
Referrals between centers fell from 28% of clients in 2020 to 8% in 2024.42
How strong: federal evaluation with a matched comparison group; the evaluators note gaps in their data.



Training alone did not move sales or hiring, even though more than 85% of trainees called it useful43
In a US trial with 4,197 applicants, free entrepreneurship training raised business ownership at first, but had no effect on sales or on having an employee, and no lasting effect for women.
More than 85% of trainees said the training was useful.43
Studies of accelerators in mostly developing countries found women-led ventures raised nearly US$100,000 less equity than men-led ones after acceleration44, and men-led startups raised 2.6 times as much additional equity after acceleration as women-led ones.45
How strong: one randomised US trial from 2003 to 2005, and one observational and one quasi-experimental study of accelerators outside the US.



Women's angel groups need a local base: two elsewhere closed for lack of members or investors46
X-Squared Angels in Columbus, Ohio, disbanded at the end of 2018 "as membership fizzled", and Golden Seeds' Philadelphia chapter shut after 2011 because there were not enough local investors.46
We found no women's angel group, angel training or women-led fund in Nebraska.
How strong: news reports from 2013 and 2019; the Nebraska absence is "not found" in our searches.



Nebraska publishes almost nothing on capital by owner gender: one figure, 41% of 17 state-backed deals47
The only published Nebraska figure we found: of 17 state-backed loans and investments under the federal State Small Business Credit Initiative from August 2022 to December 2023, 41% went to women-owned or controlled businesses.47
The Federal Reserve's small business survey has too few Nebraska responses for a state view.48
A new federal rule will collect owner gender on small business loans, but the first full year of data is due in 2029, and farm lending is left out.49
How strong: official reports and the federal rule text.



Programs limited by identity face legal challenge: one grant fund for Black women founders closed in 202450
The Fearless Fund closed its grant contest for Black women business owners after a 2024 court ruling and settlement, and another grant program paid $125,000 in legal fees to settle a similar suit.50
In October 2025 an interim federal rule removed the transportation contracting program's presumption that women-owned firms are disadvantaged; whether a final rule followed was not checked.51
Any program open only to women would need legal review.
How strong: news reports and the federal rule text; this is not legal advice.




How big each gap is


Most of the shortfall shows up before a woman ever applies for capital
No source ranks the barriers against each other, and they are measured in different ways, so this is a sense of scale, not a ranking.
Read along the path from owner to funded, hiring company: few women-owned firms have employees (see Research cited in the pitch), and most do not apply for credit (see the capital cards above).
Loan approval shows a small, unstable gap.
Venture capital shows a very large gap in share, but touches few businesses.
How strong: our reading of the research, not a single source.



Nebraska men in their own incorporated businesses earn about 1.7 times what women do52
In 2023, Nebraska men running their own incorporated businesses earned about $61,507, roughly 1.7 times women's $37,136.
Women were 33% of these business owners.52
How strong: University of Nebraska Omaha analysis; covers people self-employed in incorporated businesses only.



Women-founded firms in the US heartland got under 0.9% of US venture capital in 202053
Firms with at least one woman founder in 20 heartland states, Nebraska among them, received less than 0.9% of US venture capital in 2020.
Over five years their average deal was $1.7 million, against $3.0 million for women-founded firms nationally.53
How strong: one analysis of investment data; the 0.9% figure was checked, the deal sizes were not reviewed a second time.



Headline venture figures depend on the definition: 3% of dollars to women-only teams, 10% to mixed teams54
A 2019 count found 3% of venture dollars went to startups founded only by women and 10% to teams of women and men.54
Figures for "at least one woman founder" always run far higher than for all-women teams, so a figure is only comparable with others that use the same definition.
Our challenge packet says all-women teams got about 1% of 2025 US venture dollars; we could not open that source to check it.55
How strong: the 2019 figures were read on the publisher's page; the 2025 figure is Not checked.




Why women-owned firms stay without employees: choice or constraint?


Lower start-up capital is the largest measured reason, about 32% of the explained gap in having employees56
In the one large US breakdown we found, measured differences explained about 55% of the gap between women- and men-owned firms in having employees.
Lower start-up capital was the largest single piece (32%), prior work in a similar business added about 7%, and the choice of industry only about 4%.56
The authors cannot say whether lower start-up capital reflects borrowing limits or different plans for the business.
How strong: observational, and based on 1992 Census data, so dated.



Women start with less: 37% of women-owned firms began with under $5,000, against 30% of men-owned57
In 2012, 37% of women-owned firms started with under $5,000 against 30% of men-owned, and 3% started with $100,000 or more against 8%.
Women owners also worked fewer hours in the business: 40% worked under 20 hours a week, against 32% of men.57
Fewer hours do not explain it all: in older data, women's firms were less likely to reach $100,000 in sales at every level of hours.56
How strong: official Census survey; fewer hours can reflect both preference and caregiving.



Women-owned firms survive as often, but start with 34% lower revenue and stay smaller58
In bank data on 138,000 firms founded in 2013, women-owned firms were no more likely to close once other traits were held equal, but started with 34% lower revenue and stayed smaller.58
How strong: observational, from one bank's customers.



Motives differ, but modestly: 60% of women employer-owners call work-family balance very important, against 54% of men59
Among US owners of firms with employees in 2023, women more often called balancing work and family (60% against 54%) and flexible hours (57% against 50%) very important reasons for owning a business, and less often greater income (57% against 65%) or being their own boss (54% against 65%).59
How strong: official national survey of owners who already have employees.



No study found splits the gap into "chose not to grow" and "was held back"; women-owned startups were about 9 points less likely to make a first hire60
We searched for a study that separates choice from constraint and found none.
The one study of the step from no employees to a first employee (US startups of 2004) found women-owned startups about 9 percentage points less likely to hire within a year or two, with owner traits held equal; it does not measure motives.60
The measured drivers cut both ways: less start-up capital can mean smaller plans or less access, and fewer hours can mean preference or caregiving.
How strong: "searched, nothing found" for a direct split, limited to the searches we ran; the first-hire study is observational.




Lincoln and Nebraska in numbers


The Lincoln area has about 12,600 women-owned businesses; 13% have employees, against 23% of men-owned2
In 2023 the Lincoln metro area had about 12,600 women-owned businesses: about 1,600 with employees and about 11,000 without.
13% of them had employees, against 23% of men-owned businesses, the same pattern as across Nebraska (11% against 22%).
Lancaster County alone gives 13% against 23%.2
So the hiring gap in our pitch is not only a rural Nebraska effect.
How strong: Census counts; the counts of businesses with employees are survey estimates with about 10% sampling error for Lincoln.



Women-owned firms are 21% of Lincoln-area employers and employ about 11,200 people61
Of about 7,600 Lincoln-area businesses with employees in 2023, women-owned firms were 21%.
They employed about 11,200 people, against about 52,900 at men-owned firms.61
How strong: Census survey estimates.



Nebraskans start businesses at about three quarters of the US rate: 0.27% of adults a month, against 0.36%62
In 2025, 0.27% of Nebraska adults started a business each month, against 0.36% nationally, ranking Nebraska 35th; Nebraska has been below the US rate in every year since 2019.
Firms that do start survive well: 79% survive their first year, 14th among states.62
No state figures are published by gender because state samples are too small.
How strong: national indicators built from federal survey and administrative data; rechecked against the data files.



New business applications in Lancaster County hit 3,992 in 2025, the most since at least 200563
Business applications in Lancaster County rose from 2,435 in 2019 to 3,992 in 2025, the highest in the 2005 to 2025 series, about 12 per 1,000 residents.
Part of the rise reflects a 53-week year in 2025; on a 52-week basis the rise is about 61%.63
These counts are not split by the owner's sex.
How strong: Census administrative counts with privacy noise added; per-resident figure and the 52-week adjustment are our arithmetic.



Nebraska ranked 45th on businesses owned by women, but 3rd on businesses owned equally by women and men64
Among businesses with employees in 2018, 16% in Nebraska were owned by women (45th of 51) and 20% were owned equally by a woman and a man (3rd).64
Many Nebraska women may run businesses as co-owners, which counts of women-owned firms leave out.
How strong: Nebraska Department of Labor summary of Census survey data; covers businesses with employees only; the co-ownership reading is ours.




Who becomes a founder


The gender gap is small at "I intend to start" and widens after: 12% of US women were starting a business in 2025, against 15% of men65
In the US in 2025, 13% of women and 14% of men intended to start a business; 12% and 15% were in the process of starting one; and 6% and 8% owned a new business.65
Each month, 0.28% of women and 0.44% of men who did not own a business started one.66
So women are lost between intending and running a business, not only before intending.
How strong: two large national surveys; neither gives figures for Nebraska by gender.



Women are influenced by women: peer groups explain about half of the early-career gender gap in starting businesses67
Following about 213,000 school graduates in Norway, 11% of men and 6% of women did some entrepreneurship in their first five years.
Men were more influenced by men and women by women, and differences in peer groups explained 53% of the gap.67
In Sweden, having an entrepreneur parent raised the chance of becoming one by about 60%, and mothers passed it to daughters more strongly than fathers did.68
How strong: large observational studies outside the US.



Saying you plan to start is a leaky signal: 63% of those who did had taken no step a year later69
In a panel of adults in Austria and Finland, 63% of the 371 people who said they intended to start a business had taken no action a year later.69
How strong: observational panel outside the US.




Common beliefs, checked against the evidence

These are beliefs that came up in our pilot survey, mostly in supporters' answers on why women raise less funding, each checked against the research.10


"Fewer women start businesses": true, but the gap is bigger in growing them: women own 37% of Nebraska businesses outright but 20% of those with employees1
Of Nebraska businesses with an owner's sex recorded in 2022, 37% were owned mostly by women, 56% mostly by men and 7% equally by both; counting the equally owned ones, women own 44%.1
Only 11% of women-owned businesses had employees, against 23% of men-owned, so women own about 20% of the Nebraska businesses that employ people.1
Nationally, women also start fewer businesses: each month in 2025, 0.28% of women and 0.44% of men who did not own a business started one.66
The gap is widest among venture-funded startups: 20% of startups worldwide that raised a first funding round in 2019 had a woman among their founders.54
How strong: Census-based counts for Nebraska and a large national survey for start rates; no start rate by gender is published for Nebraska.
The 37% and the 20% are our arithmetic from the profile's counts (67,994 of 185,360 businesses; 7,494 of about 37,960 with employees).
The venture figure is global and from one database.



"Women are more risk-averse": in 54 repeats of one standard risk test, gender differences were tiny once the data were pooled70
A review of 54 repeats of one laboratory risk test, with about 7,000 people, found gender differences in fewer than 10% of studies, and "negligible in magnitude once all the data are pooled".70
A re-analysis of 35 studies found men's and women's risk-taking overlapping by more than 80%.71
This is a contested literature: other widely cited reviews report women choosing less risk on average, and we did not read them, so we call the belief overstated rather than wrong.
How strong: both reviews read at abstract level; mostly lab experiments with students, not founders.



Fear of failure does differ somewhat: 53% of US women and 46% of men said it held them back in 202472
In the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor's 2024 survey, 53% of US women and 46% of men said fear of failure held them back from starting a business (asked of adults who see good opportunities to start one).72
GEM's newest women's report finds the gap much smaller among high-potential founders and concludes that "confidence is not the biggest constraint", pointing instead to finance, networks and support.65
GEM's own reports do not fully agree on the US rate, for reasons we could not establish.
How strong: large self-reported survey; the figures do not all line up, so read them as a direction, not a precise size.



"Women don't ask": women-led firms do apply for bank credit less often, often because they expect to be turned down73
In about 6,000 small firms in 17 countries, women owners were more often discouraged from applying for bank credit where gender bias was higher, while rejection rates and loan terms did not differ.73
In Europe, women-led firms more often held back from applying, as discouraged borrowers and because more relied on their own funds.74
A US study of new founders found being female lowered the chance of asking for financing.75
The often-quoted claim that women apply for jobs only when 100% qualified and men at 60% has no published source behind it.76
How strong: observational studies; the US study read at abstract level only.
When women do reach investors, they do at least as well; see the cold-email card above and Research cited in the pitch.



"Women negotiate less": we found no study of founders negotiating terms; once women reach angel investors, 27% of their deals are funded, against 23% of all deals3
We found no study that measures how women founders negotiate investment or loan terms; that is a gap in our searches, not evidence either way.
What is measured is asking: in a US panel of people starting businesses, "being female significantly decreases the probability of asking for financing", as in the card above.75
Once women reach investors, they do at least as well: angels funded 27% of women entrepreneurs' deals in 2024, against 23% of all deals,3 and in 80,000 identical cold emails, investors replied with interest 9% more often to women.38
In the room, investors asked women more about risks and men more about gains, which fully accounted for the gender gap in funding at one major US startup competition.36
4 of the 12 supporters who answered our survey said women ask or negotiate less, have less confidence or take fewer risks.10
How strong: observational studies for asking, the US study read at abstract level only; a randomised field experiment for cold emails; the angel figures are one report's national estimates.
No study of negotiating terms was found in our searches, which were of our own notes, not a full literature search.



"More women mentors and success stories": they help women reach out, but the clearest funding lever is more women writing checks; a role-model video raised women's outreach to mentors by 57%, not their connections9
On an online mentoring platform, a short video of a successful mentoring relationship made women 57% more likely to reach out to a mentor (a relative increase), but did not raise their chance of a meaningful exchange.9
In one trial in Uganda, women entrepreneurs did better with a woman mentor;18 a second, of group mentoring on top of a cash grant, found no significant difference between men and women mentors for women, so the two trials disagree.19
In Norway, women were influenced by women: differences in peer groups explained about half (53%) of the early-career gap in starting businesses.67
For funding, the clearest lever is who writes the checks: after US venture firms hired more women investors, the share of founders who were women rose, and male investors did not become more likely to back women.6
In our survey, more women visible in pitch events, panels and classrooms, as mentors, as local success stories or as investors came up in 3 of the 12 supporters' answers; more women investors came up in fewer than 3.10
How strong: randomised trials for the video and for mentor gender (the mentor trials outside the US, with different results); large observational studies for peers (Norway) and women investors (US, read at abstract level).




Women and AI tools


Women used generative AI less than men in 17 of 18 surveys; pooled, they had about 20% lower odds of using it77
A review of surveys from 2023 and 2024 found women used generative AI less than men in every survey but one; pooling the 12 with enough data, women had about 20% lower odds of using it.77
The reasons most often measured are lower familiarity and lower confidence; even when everyone in a Kenyan study was offered the same chance to learn ChatGPT, women were about 13% less likely to want to.77
How strong: a review of published surveys, not a quality-rated systematic review.



Among small-business owners the gap is smaller: 17% of women-owned and 20% of men-owned firms paid for an AI service by the end of 202578
In Chase business-banking data, 17% of women-owned and 20% of men-owned small businesses had paid for at least one AI service by the end of 2025.
The gap was widest among the youngest owners (14% against 20%) and almost nil among the oldest.78
How strong: observational transaction data from one bank's customers.



US women have nearly caught up on ever using AI chatbots (47% against 50%), but use them less often79
In February 2026, 47% of US women and 50% of men said they ever use AI chatbots; 20% of women and 27% of men used them daily, and 35% and 40% of employed adults used them for work tasks.79
How strong: large national probability survey; the earlier year's question was worded differently, so change over time is approximate.



An AI business mentor may have helped strong businesses by over 15%, and set weaker ones back by nearly 10%80
In a trial with 640 Kenyan entrepreneurs, some were given an AI business mentor on WhatsApp.
On average it did not improve their results; high performers may have gained over 15%, while low performers did "nearly 10% worse", which the authors put down to which advice owners acted on.80
None of the AI next-step tools for founders that we reviewed publishes evidence on whether users got funded, grew, or met the person they were sent to.
How strong: randomised trial outside the US; earlier versions of the paper give different figures.




Do women owners reinvest in their communities?


In the Great Recession, women-owned US firms cut jobs up to 29% less than men-owned firms81
Privately held US firms owned by women were less likely to downsize; year-to-year job cuts were as much as 29% smaller, even after allowing for industry, size and profitability.81
How strong: observational with controls, 2005 to 2009 data; about keeping jobs in a downturn, not hiring locally.



Women-owned firms employ far more women: 48% of their full-time workers, against 28% in men-owned firms82
Across firms with five or more workers in 168 economies, 48% of full-time workers in women-owned firms were women, against 28% in men-owned firms.
Women-owned firms were smaller, though, adding fewer jobs per firm.82
How strong: descriptive World Bank survey data, not US-specific and not adjusted for other differences.



Woman-owned businesses were more than three times as likely to certify as B Corps83
Among 1,251 US firms in B Lab's records, woman-owned businesses were twice as likely to qualify for B Corp certification, which scores social and environmental performance, and more than three times as likely to certify.83
How strong: read at abstract level; compares firms already known to B Lab, not all US firms.



The popular claim that women reinvest 90% of their income in their families has no traceable study behind it84
The most specific citation we found points to a US government web page that no longer resolves; no primary study was found, and the claim is about household income, not business owners.84
Surveys of owners also find women and men give money and time to charity at similar levels, and we found no study measuring whether women owners hire, buy or bank more locally.
How strong: no study behind the 90% figure was found, so it should not be relied on.
